zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check, consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, page subset supplied in this package; CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . This is a lexical aid, not authority for this copy’s glyphs or layout.

runs.text: & fechão os olhos. i, Em breuißimo eſpaço.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's comparison with closing the eyes: the explanatory i introduces an extremely brief interval. The row begins mid-definition, not with a new headword.

Matawa is explained both as an alternative, 'or', and additively, 'also' or 'and this too'. Preserve the range of conjunctions given by the Portuguese rather than restricting it to its usual modern sense.
Matsu is a pine tree; the one-word Portuguese gloss is complete. The cedilla belongs to the historical tç spelling.
Matsuba denotes pine leaves or needles, literally the leaves of the tree named in the preceding entry.
Matsubara is a stand or grove of pines, matched by the collective Portuguese pinheiral.
Matsubune is equated with inokozuchi through the alternative marker l. The gloss merely calls it an herb of that name; it does not by itself establish a modern botanical species.
Completes cha-mada, 'called', in the preceding plant definition. This is a genuine short continuation, not an omitted entry.
Matsukaze is wind blowing against or through pines. Caje is the dictionary's historical spelling of kaze, not an anomalous personal name.

runs.text: Matçudai. l, Matdai. i, Suyeno yo.

lines.note: The paired forms denote the last age or later generations, explained by sue no yo. Renewed enlargement confirms a descending cedilla on the c of Matçudai, agreeing with the marked spelling in the example below.
Completes idade derradeira and adds perpetuity as a second interpretation. Matçu- begins the example whose sense is preserving a name for posterity.
Completes Matsudai ni na wo todomeyo to nanotte: declaring one's name so that it will remain for later generations. Keep the printed spacing and the line break inside Matçudai.

runs.text: Nomeandoſe que queria deixar nome pera os

lines.note: The Portuguese begins 'naming himself, wishing to leave a name for ...'. The scan supports Nomeandoſe, not OCR Nomcandoſe; the intended posterity appears on the following row.
Completes the translation with future generations, or forever. The rounded vowel supports vindouros rather than the OCR's vindauros.
Matsudake is defined simply as a kind of mushroom. Preserve the historical voiced spelling daqe and Portuguese cugumelos rather than replacing them with modern forms.
Matsuge means eyelashes, directly matched by pestanas dos olhos. The gue sequence represents the hard g of the Japanese word.

Matsume, with the stated uru and eta principal parts, means gathering things together. The gloss continues with things scattered or out of order, so the historical form should not be replaced by modern matomeru merely for familiarity.
Completes espalhadas, 'scattered', and adds 'without order'. Mimatçume- begins the nominal example of gathering or arranging, continued by the object particle below.
The preceding Mimatçume joins uo suru, 'perform the gathering/arranging'. Idem explicitly gives it the same meaning as the headword; uo is not part of the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Hum genero de bicho que can-

lines.note: Matsumushi is introduced as a kind of insect that sings. The definition continues below and should not be forced into a precise modern species identification.
Completes canta como grilo, 'sings like a cricket', then begins an additional small-insect sense. The second description continues on the next row.

runs.text: que ſe cria nos pinheiros, & canta como grillo

lines.note: The additional insect breeds or lives among pines and sings like a cricket. The scan supports grillo, including r and two l types, rather than OCR gillo; the earlier grilo remains singly spelled.
Saudosamente qualifies the insect's song as plaintive or wistful. It completes the preceding sentence rather than beginning a new botanical entry.
Matsu no ki is another expression for a pine tree, repeating the meaning of Matçu with the explicit word for tree.

runs.text: P. Porta feita toſcamente de ra-

lines.note: Matsu no to is a roughly made pine-branch door. Initial P. marks poetic usage; the Portuguese explanation divides ramos across the line boundary.
Completes ra-mos, specifying branches of pine as the door's material. The short row closes the poetic expression above.

runs.text: Feſta, ou ceremonias que ſe fazem,

lines.note: Matsuri is a festival or ceremonies performed for the kami named below. The terminal curved mark is a comma, comparable to the comma after ceremonias two rows below, not a word-division hyphen; the sentence continues aos Camis.
Completes the definition: ceremonies offered to the kami. Camis is the Japanese religious term with the gloss's plural ending, embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
The verb matsuri denotes holding festivals or rites. Preserve the printed abbreviated principal part u, without silently expanding it to an expected ru.
The rites include sacrifices and supplications to the kami. The spaced de precaçoens is retained; I- begins ikusagami, the war deity, in the following example.
Completes ikusagami ni chi wo matsuru, offering blood to the war deity. The Portuguese begins the equivalent 'offer, or ...', continued by sacrificar below.

runs.text: ſacrificar ao Cami da guerra o primeiro ſangue q̃

lines.note: The offering is the first enemy blood shed, sacrificed to the deity of war. The scan has guerra with two r types; preserve the printed oprimeiro spacing and the unexpanded abbreviation q̃.
Completes the first-blood translation and begins a separate example with tengu as object. This Japanese example is distinct from a Japanese term embedded inside Portuguese prose.

Completes tengu wo matsuri tsukuru, explained as ritually causing a spirit to enter someone. The Portuguese calls the spirit a demon; that is the dictionary's Christian framing, not an independent identification supplied by the reviewer.

runs.text: nio no corpo dalguem com ceremonias, ou

lines.note: Completes demo-nio and specifies entry into someone's body through ceremonies. The means of invocation continues with supplications on the next row.
Supplications complete the description of the invocation. The printed spelling here is not automatically assimilated to the spaced de precaçoens above.
Matsurigoto means government or ordinances. The initial of Gouerno is a damaged G, not OCR C; the Japanese example starts with divided Ma-.
Completes matsurigoto wo yaburu, breaking or violating ordinances. The Portuguese equivalent continues across ordena-coẽs on the next row.
Completes the phrase 'the ordinances of the kingdom'. Preserve the visible uncedilled c and the tilde on e, rather than silently regularizing the Portuguese ending.
Matsuwari is becoming entangled or entwined. The ru/atta principal parts belong to the listed verb; the metaphorical applications follow the physical comparison.
Completes enlaçar-se with ivy entwining a tree. Era is the historical spelling for ivy and naruore represents the tree phrase as printed; Per- begins the figurative-use label on the following row.
Met. completes the wholly italic Per-met. figurative-use marker. Matsuwatta hito describes an entangling or troublesome person; the Portuguese continues with embarrassments and tricks.
Completes embaraços and adds trapaças, 'tricks' or 'frauds'. The next example begins a description of tangled or misleading statements.

runs.text: Dizer couſas que não ſe entendẽ,

lines.note: Completes matsuwatta koto wo yuu, saying things that cannot be understood. The damaged final Japanese form is yǔ, with a visible caron, rather than the OCR's yfi; the Portuguese identifies it as the verb 'say'.

runs.text: ou impor a alguem o que não he, &c.

lines.note: Adds the alternative of attributing something untrue to another person. This completes the misleading-speech example rather than the next pine-related noun.
Matsuyama is glossed as a pine wood or thicket. Although yama can suggest a mountain, the Portuguese here specifies vegetation, not a place name.
Matsuyani is pine resin or pitch. The headword's damaged vowel is compatible with yani; there is no basis for replacing the historical spelling with a modernized form.
Matdai repeats the later-age or perpetual sense, explained by sue no yo. The scan supports t in Matdai and the separate words Derradeira idade; the Portuguese phrase continues at the top of column 2.
Completes pe-ra sempre, 'forever', then begins the saying 'a person lasts one lifetime; a name ...'. The divided mat- belongs to matdai on the next row.

runs.text: O homẽ dura hũa idade, o no-

lines.note: Completes the saying 'a person has one lifetime, a name endures for later ages'. Yax. is the upright printed citation label; the Portuguese contrasts a human lifespan with the persistence of a name.
Completes no-me, stating that the name remains forever. This closes the cross-column Matdai entry.
Mate is a kind of shellfish, also called mategai. The alternative Japanese name belongs to the same definition and remains upright.
Idem explicitly assigns Mategai the same shellfish meaning. It is a short continuation of the preceding row, not an additional missing headword.
Matgo denotes the hour of death. The example begins matgo no iccu, a deathbed utterance; the scan supports ic-, not the OCR's ie-, with the doubled consonant completed below.

runs.text: Sentença, ou outras palauras que hum

lines.note: Cu completes iccu, a verse or utterance. The Portuguese describes a sentence or other words spoken by someone, with the deathbed circumstance supplied on the next row.
Completes the definition of the deathbed utterance: words said at the hour of death. It belongs to Matgono iccu rather than the following temple entry.
Matsuji is a dependent temple, explained by sue no tera. Tera within the Portuguese definition is visibly upright as a whole word; the former mixed T/era styling did not match the printed type.

runs.text: ganea a outra principal como fregueſia em com-

lines.note: Completes sufraganea, describing a temple subordinate to a principal one. The missionary analogy compares that relationship with a parish and its cathedral.
Completes comparação da see, the cathedral comparison. The scan supports two e types in the historical see, not OCR sce; no accent is supplied from modern sé.
This separate homophonous Matji is explained by sue no toki, the last time or hour. It must not be merged with the preceding dependent-temple entry.

runs.text: Aluo que ſe poem na barreira. ¶

lines.note: Mato is the target set up at a shooting range. Ma- begins the example of shooting at that target.
Completes mato wo iru, to shoot at the target, and starts mato ni ataru below. Preserve the visibly separated a o in the Portuguese gloss.
Mato ni ataru means hitting the target. The next example, mato wo ihazusu, contrasts missing it; the scan retains the close Acertarno word spacing and the divided Japanese spelling.
Completes ifaz-zuſu, missing the target. The long s is visible in the final syllable; the two z letters straddle the physical line break.
Matoba is the place where people shoot at targets, an archery or shooting range. This names the location rather than another kind of target.
Matocana describes a rounded, solid thing, compared with a globe. The following example extends solidity or wholeness to a person's character.
Completes glo-bo and introduces matocana hito, a person characterized by solidity or integrity. The Portuguese noun homem continues with its qualifications below.
The person is 'solid and whole', here expressing dependable integrity. The two adjectives complete the human example rather than the preceding physical comparison alone.
Matocani is identified as the adverb corresponding to Matocana. Adu. supplies the grammatical relationship even though no separate Portuguese paraphrase follows.
Matǒdo is a simple, upright person. The caron is visible; the Portuguese includes the i of ſimples, lost in OCR ſmples.
Matoi means wrapping or enveloping. Both abbreviated long-vowel forms have circumflexes, in contrast with the caron of Matǒdo immediately above.
The added sense is putting on clothing. The t is present in Veſtir; Tçuri ſuru ama- begins an example involving people fishing.
Completes amabito ni magirete, mingling or disguising oneself among fishermen, and begins wearing a torn straw cloak on one's body. The final mi- continues as mini below.
Completes mi ni matoi, putting the cloak on. Taif. is the upright source label followed by italic Lib. 29; the Portuguese translation begins the divided Disfraçado.

runs.text: fraçado com os peſcadores viſtio hũa capa de pa

lines.note: The translation describes disguising oneself among fishermen and putting on a straw cloak. Preserve the printed Dis-fraçado order and the unhyphenated pa at the physical edge rather than supplying an expected line-end mark.
Completes pa-lha rota, a torn straw cloak. The absence of a printed hyphen on the preceding row does not alter the continuity of the word.
Matowari denotes becoming wrapped or entangled. The Portuguese continues the reflexive trauar-se on the next physical line.

runs.text: ſe hũa couſa cõ outra. Vide,

lines.note: Completes the sense of one thing becoming entangled with another and refers the reader to Matçuuari. Preserve the abbreviated cõ and the cross-reference's printed principal part u.

runs.text: Matouono. l, madouono coromo. Meno a-

lines.note: Matouono and madouono coromo name the garment explained by me no arai nuno, cloth with a coarse or open weave. Preserve the different t/d spellings in the paired forms.
Completes me no arai nuno and gives the material as coarse linen or hemp cloth. The historical canemo and the printed double-s sort in großo are retained.
Ralo completes the coarse, loosely woven garment description. The closing P. marks poetic usage, not another Japanese word.

runs.text: Frecha com que ſe atira à barreira.

lines.note: Matoya is an arrow used for target shooting. Preserve the historical Portuguese Frecha rather than modernizing it to flecha.
Mattaku means certainly or completely. The initial t of totalmen- is abraded but has compatible surviving ink; the OCR's eotalmen- does not represent the printed word.
Completes totalmente and adds perfeitamente, 'perfectly'. These are the adverbial meanings of Mattacu, not a fresh headword.
Mattai describes something whole or intact. Kizu tsukanu begins the example of a pear without damage, continued below.
Completes the negative example: there is not even one whole, unblemished pear. Naxi is the pear noun here, distinct from the final negative nai.

runs.text: ſò pera inteira ſem lesão ficou.

lines.note: The translation confirms that not a single intact, undamaged pear remained. The apparently repetitive inteira and sem lesão both belong to the printed explanation.
Mattô is equated with atama, 'head', with the upright B. usage label. The entire label is roman; Acu- begins the example about dirty water.
Completes akusui mattō ni sosogu, pouring dirty water over the head. Both long-s types in ſoſoqu are retained and the translation continues below.
Completes sobre a cabeça, 'over the head'. This closes the example of Mattô as a noun.
A separate Mattô is the adverb 'entirely'. The repeated spelling does not license merging it with the preceding head noun.
Unaccented Matto means 'a little more'. The contrast with Mattô above is visibly printed and semantically meaningful.
Mat yô means descendants, with Bat yô recommended as the preferable form. Preserve the source's Deſendentes without inserting a c and the visible grave accent in Meliùs.

Matza, preferably Batza, is explained by sue no za, the last or lowest seat. The damaged label supports Melius rather than OCR Mecius; its accent area is too abraded to add a grave securely, so the unaccented baseline is retained.

Completes derradeiro assento, the lowest seat in the zashiki or formal room. Zaxiqui occurs within the Portuguese explanation and is retained in its observed typeface for optional human whole-word review.
